editorial:
Imagine opening a giant old shoebox filled with family photos, home movies, and old TV clips from a city you love. That is exactly how this film feels. You get to travel through seventy years of life in Beirut, Lebanon, seeing everything from happy parties and quiet moments to the scary parts of war. Since Lebanon does not have one official national archive, director Lana Daher puts together a beautiful puzzle using footage from regular people, artists, and filmmakers. It feels less like a history lesson and more like a warm, personal letter to a city that has been through so much but still knows how to dance.

What really hits home is how the film captures the raw emotion of the people. You will see a mix of high-energy celebration and deep sadness that keeps you hooked. The pacing is smooth, though some might find the lack of a traditional plot a bit slow at times. If you enjoy seeing how people lived in the past, you should definitely check this out. For the best experience, try streaming it in 4K Ultra HD on Prime Video to see the archival details clearly, or rent it on Apple TV for a cozy movie night at home.
endingExplained: The film wraps up by showing that memory is the only thing that cannot be destroyed. In the final scenes, you see a blend of the oldest footage and the newest clips, proving that Beirut always finds a way to start over. It ends with a hopeful message about how art and filming are ways to fight back against forgetting. You leave the movie feeling that love for your home is the strongest bond of all.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves history, travel, and human stories.
